common_name: Resurrection Plant (Rose of Jericho, False Rose of Jericho)

planting.note: Set whole rosettes or offsets on top of a shallow dish of gritty, fast-draining substrate rather than burying them, and keep in bright indirect light with only intermittent misting or soaking.

directions: Rather than planting in ground soil, rest the rosette on gritty, sharply drained substrate and allow it to dry fully between soakings, since it is native to sun-baked limestone outcrops of the Chihuahuan Desert of Texas and northern Mexico. When dry, the fronds curl tightly inward into a brown, seemingly dead ball that can survive years of complete desiccation; a thorough soaking uncurls the rosette within hours and restores its green color, a spectacle that has made it a popular novelty and terrarium curiosity. Give bright, filtered light rather than deep shade, since it needs light to resume photosynthesis once rehydrated, and never let it sit in standing water or heavy, moisture-retentive soil.

planting.note: Divide established clumps or pot offsets into a coarse, well-drained bark- or fern-fiber-based mix in filtered shade; whisk fern often colonizes the base of palm trunks and tree fern trunks and appreciates a similarly airy, epiphyte-style rooting medium.

directions: Plant divisions in a coarse, fast-draining, bark-rich mix in dappled shade at the base of palms, tree ferns, or in rock crevices, where it naturally grows as an epiphyte or lithophyte in subtropical and tropical regions worldwide, including Florida and Hawaii. Psilotum nudum is one of the most primitive living vascular plants, with no true leaves or roots — only repeatedly forking, bright green photosynthetic stems studded with small yellow spore-bearing knobs, giving it a spare, architectural, almost otherworldly texture. It tolerates neglect and brief dry spells once established but colors best and spreads most readily with consistent humidity and filtered light. Use it as a curious textural accent among ferns and mosses in a shaded subtropical bed or greenhouse epiphyte mount.

planting.note: Mount or pot stem cuttings and offsets in a chunky, orchid-bark epiphyte mix and hang or place in bright, filtered shade with high humidity, mimicking its natural perch on tropical tree trunks and mossy rock faces.

directions: Grow in a chunky, well-aerated epiphyte mix of bark and sphagnum in a hanging basket or mounted on a fern totem in bright, filtered shade, since Huperzia squarrosa grows naturally as an epiphyte on trees and mossy cliffs throughout tropical Asia and the Pacific. Its long, trailing, densely leaved stems of narrow, glossy, dark green scale-like foliage arch and cascade to form a shaggy, tassel-like curtain, with slender upright spore-bearing tips giving the plant its common name. It demands consistently high humidity and evenly moist (never soggy) roots, browning quickly if allowed to dry out for extended periods. Best suited to a shaded greenhouse, conservatory, or humid outdoor shade garden in frost-free climates.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in wet, calcareous, gritty soil or a submerged container in partial shade in spring; like other horsetails it spreads by rhizome and should be confined with buried edging or grown in a pot to prevent it colonizing surrounding wet ground.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in consistently wet, gritty, mineral-rich soil at a pond margin or in a submerged container in partial shade to full sun; this circumboreal species tolerates far colder winters than common horsetail and thrives in calcareous fens, dune slacks, and gravelly stream banks across the northern hemisphere. Slender, evergreen, ridged stems are distinctly banded in green and near-black at each joint with a fine white margin, giving a crisper, more refined look than the taller Equisetum hyemale, making it well suited to small water features and alpine-style bog plantings. Confine the rhizomes firmly, since even this dwarf species spreads steadily wherever soil stays reliably moist.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in moist, humus-rich soil in deep shade or bright indirect light in zone 10-12 or as a terrarium plant; Ruby Spikemoss needs consistently high humidity and dislikes both drying out and standing water.

directions: Root stem cuttings in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in deep shade with very high humidity, replicating the rainforest floor of Central and South America where this creeping fern ally naturally grows. The upper leaf surface has a metallic, iridescent blue-green sheen produced by structural coloration, while the undersides and new growth flush a striking deep ruby red, giving the mat-forming foliage an unusual two-toned shimmer as light shifts across it. It is far more heat- and humidity-loving than most cultivated selaginellas and rarely tolerates temperatures below 60°F, so it is best grown as a terrarium or shaded greenhouse groundcover outside the wet tropics. Keep the growing medium constantly moist and never allow it to dry out even briefly.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated rooted stem sections into wet, acidic, sandy or peaty soil kept saturated in partial shade to full sun in spring; bog clubmoss is a pioneer of open, disturbed wet-sand habitats and rarely persists where taller vegetation closes in around it.

directions: Plant rooted stem sections into permanently wet, acidic, sandy or peaty soil in a bog garden or pond-margin planting kept in partial shade, mimicking the open, sunny to lightly shaded wet-sand and peat habitats where this circumboreal species is found. Low, creeping, forking stems of soft yellow-green, needle-like leaves hug the ground and root as they spread, sending up short, erect, cone-tipped fertile branches in late summer. As a pioneer species it colonizes bare, saturated sand and peat most readily and tends to decline once competing vegetation fills in around it, so it pairs well with sundews and other open-bog specialists. Keep the substrate constantly saturated and nutrient-poor, since it is adapted to acidic, low-fertility wetland margins.
